questions.question: A bipartite graph has 50 tasks on one side and 40 servers on the other. What can you say about perfect matchings?
options: None can exist, because the sides have different sizes
One exists if every task connects to some server
One always exists in a bipartite graph
It depends on the edge weights
questions.explanation: Every matching edge uses one vertex from each side, so at most 40 tasks can be covered. A perfect matching needs equal sides.

questions.question: In a stable-matching instance, evaluator E rejected applicant A on day 3. What does the key invariant tell you about the final matching?
options: A ends up with their last choice
E ends up with someone E prefers to A
E and A form a rogue pair
questions.explanation: Evaluators only keep or trade up, so after rejecting A, E always holds someone better. That is exactly why (E, A) can't be rogue.

questions.question: Why does the 'everyone gets a partner' proof fail if there are more applicants than evaluators?
options: The contradiction relied on there being too few other applicants to fill all n evaluators
questions.explanation: The proof says all n evaluators would need partners better than A, but only n − 1 others exist. With more applicants, that count no longer runs out, and someone really can be left out.

questions.question: Gale-Shapley with doctors proposing gives doctor D the hospital H. What does the optimality theorem say?
options: H also got its first choice
No stable matching gives D a hospital D prefers to H
questions.explanation: Proposers get their best FEASIBLE partner: the best they could have in any stable matching. That may not be their first choice.
